1	# External Agent Plugin Protocol
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	The Entire CLI supports external agent plugins — standalone binaries that implement the Agent interface via a subcommand-based protocol over stdin/stdout. This allows third-party agents to integrate with the CLI without modifying the main repository.
6	
7	## Discovery
8	
9	The CLI discovers external agents by scanning `$PATH` for executables matching the pattern `entire-agent-<name>`. For example, `entire-agent-cursor` would register as the "cursor" agent.
10	
11	- Binaries whose `<name>` conflicts with an already-registered built-in agent are skipped.
12	- Discovery runs once during CLI initialization (before building the hooks command tree).
13	- The binary must be executable and respond to the `info` subcommand.
14	
15	## Environment
16	
17	Every subcommand invocation sets:
18	
19	| Variable | Description |
20	|---|---|
21	| `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT` | Absolute path to the git repository root |
22	| `ENTIRE_PROTOCOL_VERSION` | Protocol version (`1`) |
23	
24	The working directory is set to the repository root.
25	
26	## Communication Model
27	
28	- **Subcommand-based:** Each Agent interface method maps to a CLI subcommand.
29	- **JSON over stdin/stdout:** Structured data uses JSON. Transcripts use raw bytes.
30	- **Stateless:** Each invocation is independent — no persistent connection.
31	- **Exit codes:** `0` = success, non-zero = error. Error messages go to stderr.
32	
33	## Subcommands
34	
35	### Always Required
36	
37	#### `info`
38	
39	Returns agent metadata and declared capabilities.
40	
41	**Arguments:** None
42	
43	**Output (stdout):** JSON
44	
45	```json
46	{
47	  "protocol_version": 1,
48	  "name": "cursor",
49	  "type": "Cursor",
50	  "description": "Cursor - AI-powered code editor",
51	  "is_preview": true,
52	  "protected_dirs": [".cursor"],
53	  "hook_names": ["session-start", "session-end", "stop"],
54	  "capabilities": {
55	    "hooks": true,
56	    "transcript_analyzer": true,
57	    "compact_transcript": true,
58	    "transcript_preparer": false,
59	    "token_calculator": false,
60	    "text_generator": false,
61	    "hook_response_writer": false,
62	    "subagent_aware_extractor": false
63	  }
64	}
65	```
66	
67	The `capabilities` object determines which optional subcommands the CLI will call. If a capability is `false` or missing, the CLI will never invoke the corresponding subcommands.
68	
69	#### `detect`
70	
71	Checks whether the agent is present/usable in the current environment.
72	
73	**Arguments:** None
74	
75	**Output (stdout):** JSON
76	
77	```json
78	{"present": true}
79	```
80	
81	#### `get-session-id`
82	
83	Extracts the session ID from a hook input event.
84	
85	**Input (stdin):** JSON — the [HookInput object](#hookinput-object)
86	
87	**Output (stdout):** JSON
88	
89	```json
90	{"session_id": "abc123"}
91	```
92	
93	#### `get-session-dir --repo-path <path>`
94	
95	Returns the directory where agent sessions are stored.
96	
97	**Arguments:**
98	- `--repo-path` — Absolute path to the repository
99	
100	**Output (stdout):** JSON
101	
102	```json
103	{"session_dir": "/path/to/sessions"}
104	```
105	
106	#### `resolve-session-file --session-dir <dir> --session-id <id>`
107	
108	Resolves the session file path from a session directory and ID.
109	
110	**Arguments:**
111	- `--session-dir` — Session directory path
112	- `--session-id` — Session identifier
113	
114	**Output (stdout):** JSON
115	
116	```json
117	{"session_file": "/path/to/session/file.jsonl"}
118	```
119	
120	#### `read-session`
121	
122	Reads session data from a hook input event.
123	
124	**Input (stdin):** JSON — the [HookInput object](#hookinput-object)
125	
126	**Output (stdout):** JSON — [AgentSession object](#agentsession-object)
127	
128	```json
129	{
130	  "session_id": "abc123",
131	  "agent_name": "cursor",
132	  "repo_path": "/path/to/repo",
133	  "session_ref": "/path/to/file.jsonl",
134	  "start_time": "2026-01-13T12:00:00Z",
135	  "native_data": null,
136	  "modified_files": ["src/main.go"],
137	  "new_files": [],
138	  "deleted_files": []
139	}
140	```
141	
142	#### `write-session`
143	
144	Writes/updates session data.
145	
146	**Input (stdin):** JSON — the [AgentSession object](#agentsession-object)
147	
148	**Output:** Exit 0 on success.
149	
150	#### `read-transcript --session-ref <path>`
151	
152	Reads a transcript file and returns its raw bytes.
153	
154	**Arguments:**
155	- `--session-ref` — Path to the transcript file
156	
157	**Output (stdout):** Raw transcript bytes.
158	
159	#### `chunk-transcript --max-size <n>`
160	
161	Splits a transcript into chunks for storage.
162	
163	**Input (stdin):** Raw transcript bytes.
164	
165	**Arguments:**
166	- `--max-size` — Maximum chunk size in bytes
167	
168	**Output (stdout):** JSON
169	
170	```json
171	{"chunks": ["<base64-encoded-chunk>", "..."]}
172	```
173	
174	#### `reassemble-transcript`
175	
176	Reassembles transcript chunks back into a full transcript.
177	
178	**Input (stdin):** JSON
179	
180	```json
181	{"chunks": ["<base64-encoded-chunk>", "..."]}
182	```
183	
184	**Output (stdout):** Raw transcript bytes.
185	
186	#### `format-resume-command --session-id <id>`
187	
188	Returns the command a user can run to resume a session.
189	
190	**Arguments:**
191	- `--session-id` — Session identifier
192	
193	**Output (stdout):** JSON
194	
195	```json
196	{"command": "cursor --resume abc123"}
197	```
198	
199	### Capability: `hooks`
200	
201	These subcommands are required when `capabilities.hooks` is `true`.
202	
203	#### `parse-hook --hook <name>`
204	
205	Parses a raw agent hook payload into a structured event.
206	
207	**Arguments:**
208	- `--hook` — Hook name (e.g., "stop", "session-start")
209	
210	**Input (stdin):** Raw agent hook payload bytes.
211	
212	**Output (stdout):** JSON — the parsed [Event object](#event-object), or `null` if the payload is not relevant.
213	
214	#### `install-hooks [--local-dev] [--force]`
215	
216	Installs agent hooks for Entire integration.
217	
218	**Arguments:**
219	- `--local-dev` — Use local development binary path (optional)
220	- `--force` — Overwrite existing hooks (optional)
221	
222	**Output (stdout):** JSON
223	
224	```json
225	{"hooks_installed": 3}
226	```
227	
228	#### `uninstall-hooks`
229	
230	Removes installed agent hooks.
231	
232	**Arguments:** None
233	
234	**Output:** Exit 0 on success.
235	
236	#### `are-hooks-installed`
237	
238	Checks whether hooks are currently installed.
239	
240	**Arguments:** None
241	
242	**Output (stdout):** JSON
243	
244	```json
245	{"installed": true}
246	```
247	
248	### Capability: `transcript_analyzer`
249	
250	Required when `capabilities.transcript_analyzer` is `true`.
251	
252	#### `get-transcript-position --path <path>`
253	
254	Returns the current byte position/size of a transcript file.
255	
256	**Arguments:**
257	- `--path` — Path to the transcript file
258	
259	**Output (stdout):** JSON
260	
261	```json
262	{"position": 12345}
263	```
264	
265	#### `extract-modified-files --path <path> --offset <n>`
266	
267	Extracts the list of files modified by the agent from a transcript.
268	
269	**Arguments:**
270	- `--path` — Path to the transcript file
271	- `--offset` — Byte offset to start reading from
272	
273	**Output (stdout):** JSON
274	
275	```json
276	{"files": ["path/to/file1.go", "path/to/file2.go"], "current_position": 12345}
277	```
278	
279	The `current_position` field returns the transcript position after extraction, allowing the caller to resume from that point on subsequent calls.
280	
281	#### `extract-prompts --session-ref <path> --offset <n>`
282	
283	Extracts user prompts from a transcript.
284	
285	**Arguments:**
286	- `--session-ref` — Path to the transcript file
287	- `--offset` — Byte offset to start reading from
288	
289	**Output (stdout):** JSON
290	
291	```json
292	{"prompts": ["first prompt text", "second prompt text"]}
293	```
294	
295	#### `extract-summary --session-ref <path>`
296	
297	Extracts an AI-generated summary from a transcript.
298	
299	**Arguments:**
300	- `--session-ref` — Path to the transcript file
301	
302	**Output (stdout):** JSON
303	
304	```json
305	{"summary": "Summary text here", "has_summary": true}
306	```
307	
308	### Capability: `transcript_preparer`
309	
310	Required when `capabilities.transcript_preparer` is `true`.
311	
312	#### `prepare-transcript --session-ref <path>`
313	
314	Prepares/processes a transcript file (e.g., converting from raw format).
315	
316	**Arguments:**
317	- `--session-ref` — Path to the transcript file
318	
319	**Output:** Exit 0 on success.
320	
321	### Capability: `compact_transcript`
322	
323	Required when `capabilities.compact_transcript` is `true`.
324	
325	#### `compact-transcript --session-ref <path>`
326	
327	Builds a compact transcript representation for checkpoints v2.
328	
329	**Arguments:**
330	- `--session-ref` — Path to the transcript file
331	
332	**Output (stdout):** JSON
333	
334	```json
335	{
336	  "transcript": "eyJ0eXBlIjoiLi4uIn0K",
337	  "assets": [
338	    {
339	      "name": "image-1.png",
340	      "media_type": "image/png",
341	      "data": "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAA..."
342	    }
343	  ]
344	}
345	```
346	
347	The `transcript` field is required and must contain base64-encoded `transcript.jsonl` bytes.
348	
349	Those bytes must be the complete cumulative compact **Entire Transcript Format** JSONL for the session up to the current point in time (not a delta/scoped slice since the previous checkpoint).
350	
351	The CLI writes these bytes byte-for-byte as the full `transcript.jsonl` file for the checkpoint, so external agents must always return the entire compact transcript accumulated so far.
352	
353	Those bytes must satisfy the checkpoints v2 format requirements:
354	
355	- UTF-8 JSONL, written byte-for-byte by the CLI to `transcript.jsonl`
356	- Newline-terminated JSONL: each record must end with `\n`, including the final record
357	- Every line includes format metadata (`v`, `agent`, `cli_version`) alongside the entry data
358	- Supported top-level entry types are currently:
359	  - `user`
360	  - `assistant`
361	
362	`user` entries use `content` as an array of user blocks, typically text and optionally images:
363	
364	```json
365	{"v":1,"agent":"opencode","cli_version":"0.42.0","type":"user","ts":"2026-01-13T12:00:00Z","content":[{"text":"Fix the login bug"}]}
366	```
367	
368	`assistant` entries use `content` as either a string or an array of assistant blocks. They may optionally include `input_tokens` and `output_tokens` fields for token usage tracking. The structured array form supports at least:
369	
370	- `{"type":"text","text":"..."}`
371	- `{"type":"tool_use","id":"...","name":"...","input":{...}}`
372	
373	Tool output is represented inline on the preceding `tool_use` block via an optional `result` object (there is no separate top-level `user_tool_result` entry):
374	
375	- `"result": {"output":"...","status":"success|error", ...}`
376	
377	Examples:
378	
379	```json
380	{"v":1,"agent":"opencode","cli_version":"0.42.0","type":"user","ts":"2026-01-13T12:00:00Z","content":[{"text":"Fix the login bug"}]}
381	{"v":1,"agent":"opencode","cli_version":"0.42.0","type":"assistant","ts":"2026-01-13T12:00:02Z","id":"msg_123","input_tokens":150,"output_tokens":42,"content":[{"type":"text","text":"I updated the file."},{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_123","name":"Read","input":{"file_path":"src/main.go"},"result":{"output":"package main","status":"success","file":{"filePath":"src/main.go","numLines":1}}}]}
382	```
383	
384	For complete examples of the expected output format, see the [compact transcript test fixtures](../../cmd/entire/cli/transcript/compact/testdata/).
385	
386	The compact transcript should exclude agent-native envelope/progress/system noise and retain only the normalized content needed by Entire's checkpoint readers.
387	
388	The optional `assets` field is reserved for externalized checkpoint assets. Each asset object contains:
389	
390	| Field | Type | Description |
391	|---|---|---|
392	| `name` | string | Asset filename |
393	| `media_type` | string | MIME type for the asset |
394	| `data` | string | Base64-encoded asset bytes |
395	
396	Current CLI behavior:
397	- If `compact_transcript` is missing or `false`, the CLI will skip compact transcript generation for that external agent, fall back to raw transcript storage, and log a warning.
398	- If `compact-transcript` fails or returns invalid output, the CLI will also fall back to raw transcript storage and log a warning.
399	- The CLI normalizes `transcript` bytes by appending a trailing newline when missing, and treats whitespace-only transcript output as invalid.
400	- If `assets` are returned, the CLI accepts them in the protocol shape but currently ignores them for storage and read paths.
401	
402	### Capability: `token_calculator`
403	
404	Required when `capabilities.token_calculator` is `true`.
405	
406	#### `calculate-tokens --offset <n>`
407	
408	Calculates token usage from a transcript.
409	
410	**Input (stdin):** Raw transcript bytes.
411	
412	**Arguments:**
413	- `--offset` — Byte offset to start calculating from
414	
415	**Output (stdout):** JSON
416	
417	```json
418	{
419	  "input_tokens": 1500,
420	  "cache_creation_tokens": 0,
421	  "cache_read_tokens": 200,
422	  "output_tokens": 500,
423	  "api_call_count": 3,
424	  "subagent_tokens": null
425	}
426	```
427	
428	Only `input_tokens` and `output_tokens` are required. The optional fields (`cache_creation_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`, `api_call_count`) default to `0` if omitted. `subagent_tokens` is an optional nested object with the same structure, for agents that spawn subagents.
429	
430	### Capability: `text_generator`
431	
432	Required when `capabilities.text_generator` is `true`.
433	
434	External agents that declare `capabilities.text_generator: true` can be used as
435	summary providers for `entire explain --generate` and checkpoint auto-summarize.
436	Configure them with:
437	
438	```bash
439	entire configure --summarize-provider <agent-name> [--summarize-model <model>]
440	```
441	
442	The provider name is derived from the executable name `entire-agent-<agent-name>`.
443	The CLI passes Entire's summary prompt on stdin to `generate-text --model <model>`
444	and expects `{"text":"..."}` on stdout.
445	
446	#### `generate-text --model <model>`
447	
448	Generates text using the agent's underlying LLM.
449	
450	**Input (stdin):** Prompt text.
451	
452	**Arguments:**
453	- `--model` — Model to use for generation
454	
455	**Output (stdout):** JSON
456	
457	```json
458	{"text": "Generated response text"}
459	```
460	
461	### Capability: `hook_response_writer`
462	
463	Required when `capabilities.hook_response_writer` is `true`.
464	
465	#### `write-hook-response --message <message>`
466	
467	Writes a message in the agent's native hook response format.
468	
469	**Arguments:**
470	- `--message` — Message to write
471	
472	**Output (stdout):** Agent-native format bytes (e.g., JSONL for Claude Code).
473	
474	### Capability: `subagent_aware_extractor`
475	
476	Required when `capabilities.subagent_aware_extractor` is `true`.
477	
478	#### `extract-all-modified-files --offset <n> --subagents-dir <dir>`
479	
480	Extracts modified files from both the main transcript and any subagent transcripts.
481	
482	**Input (stdin):** Raw main transcript bytes.
483	
484	**Arguments:**
485	- `--offset` — Byte offset for the main transcript
486	- `--subagents-dir` — Directory containing subagent transcripts
487	
488	**Output (stdout):** JSON
489	
490	```json
491	{"files": ["file1.go", "file2.go"]}
492	```
493	
494	#### `calculate-total-tokens --offset <n> --subagents-dir <dir>`
495	
496	Calculates total token usage across main transcript and subagent transcripts.
497	
498	**Input (stdin):** Raw main transcript bytes.
499	
500	**Arguments:**
501	- `--offset` — Byte offset for the main transcript
502	- `--subagents-dir` — Directory containing subagent transcripts
503	
504	**Output (stdout):** JSON
505	
506	```json
507	{
508	  "input_tokens": 5000,
509	  "cache_creation_tokens": 0,
510	  "cache_read_tokens": 1000,
511	  "output_tokens": 2000,
512	  "api_call_count": 8,
513	  "subagent_tokens": {
514	    "input_tokens": 2000,
515	    "output_tokens": 800
516	  }
517	}
518	```
519	
520	Same token usage format as `calculate-tokens`. The `subagent_tokens` field aggregates usage from all subagents.

522	## Shared Object Definitions
523	
524	### HookInput Object
525	
526	The HookInput object is passed via stdin to `get-session-id` and `read-session`.
527	
528	```json
529	{
530	  "hook_type": "stop",
531	  "session_id": "abc123",
532	  "session_ref": "/path/to/transcript.jsonl",
533	  "timestamp": "2026-01-13T12:00:00Z",
534	  "user_prompt": "Fix the login bug",
535	  "tool_name": "Write",
536	  "tool_use_id": "toolu_abc123",
537	  "tool_input": {"path": "/src/main.go"},
538	  "raw_data": {"custom_field": "value"}
539	}
540	```
541	
542	| Field | Type | Description |
543	|---|---|---|
544	| `hook_type` | string | Hook type: `session_start`, `session_end`, `user_prompt_submit`, `stop`, `pre_tool_use`, `post_tool_use` |
545	| `session_id` | string | Agent session identifier |
546	| `session_ref` | string | Agent-specific session reference (typically a file path) |
547	| `timestamp` | string | RFC 3339 timestamp |
548	| `user_prompt` | string | User's prompt text (from `user_prompt_submit` hooks). Optional. |
549	| `tool_name` | string | Tool name (from `pre_tool_use`/`post_tool_use` hooks). Optional. |
550	| `tool_use_id` | string | Tool invocation ID. Optional. |
551	| `tool_input` | object | Raw tool input JSON. Optional. |
552	| `raw_data` | object | Agent-specific data for extension. Optional. |
553	
554	### AgentSession Object
555	
556	Used as input to `write-session` and output from `read-session`.
557	
558	```json
559	{
560	  "session_id": "abc123",
561	  "agent_name": "cursor",
562	  "repo_path": "/path/to/repo",
563	  "session_ref": "/path/to/transcript.jsonl",
564	  "start_time": "2026-01-13T12:00:00Z",
565	  "native_data": null,
566	  "modified_files": ["src/main.go"],
567	  "new_files": ["src/new_file.go"],
568	  "deleted_files": []
569	}
570	```
571	
572	| Field | Type | Description |
573	|---|---|---|
574	| `session_id` | string | Agent session identifier |
575	| `agent_name` | string | Agent registry name |
576	| `repo_path` | string | Absolute path to the repository |
577	| `session_ref` | string | Path/reference to session in agent's storage |
578	| `start_time` | string | RFC 3339 timestamp of session start |
579	| `native_data` | bytes/null | Session content in agent's native format (opaque to CLI) |
580	| `modified_files` | string[] | Files modified during the session |
581	| `new_files` | string[] | Files created during the session |
582	| `deleted_files` | string[] | Files deleted during the session |

584	### Event Object
585	
586	Returned by `parse-hook`. Represents a normalized lifecycle event.
587	
588	```json
589	{
590	  "type": 3,
591	  "session_id": "abc123",
592	  "session_ref": "/path/to/transcript.jsonl",
593	  "prompt": "Fix the login bug",
594	  "model": "claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
595	  "timestamp": "2026-01-13T12:00:00Z"
596	}
597	```
598	
599	| Field | Type | Description |
600	|---|---|---|
601	| `type` | int | **Required.** Event type (see table below) |
602	| `session_id` | string | **Required.** Agent session identifier |
603	| `previous_session_id` | string | Non-empty when this event represents a session continuation/handoff. Optional. |
604	| `session_ref` | string | Agent-specific transcript reference. Optional. |
605	| `prompt` | string | User's prompt text (on `TurnStart` events). Optional. |
606	| `model` | string | LLM model identifier. Optional. |
607	| `timestamp` | string | RFC 3339 timestamp. Optional. |

137	func stripExeExt(name string) string {

139		case ".exe", ".bat", ".cmd":

Now I have the picture. Two things to call out:

**This is a different mechanism than external agents.** The existing system (`entire-agent-<name>` binaries) implements a 15+ subcommand JSON protocol (`info`, `detect`, `parse-hook`, `compact-transcript`, …) discovered in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/external/discovery.go:69`. That's not what you want for `entire-pgr`.

What you're describing is **git-style command extension**: `entire pgr <args>` → `exec("entire-pgr", args...)` with stdin/stdout/stderr/exit-code passthrough, no protocol. Like `git foo` → `git-foo`, `kubectl foo` → `kubectl-foo`.

What's needed:

1. **Separate prefix and discovery** — keep `entire-agent-*` reserved for the protocol, use `entire-*` (excluding `entire-agent-*`) for passthrough plugins. Otherwise the agent discovery will try to call `entire-pgr info` and skip it when JSON parsing fails.
2. **Lazy resolution in root command** — Cobra errors on unknown subcommands by default. Either intercept args in `main.go` before `root.Execute()`, or set the root's `RunE`/`Args` to dispatch unknown first-arg → `exec.LookPath("entire-" + arg)`. Built-ins must win on collision.
3. **Disable flag parsing on the dispatch path** — so `entire pgr --foo` passes `--foo` through verbatim instead of Cobra rejecting it. `DisableFlagParsing: true` + `Args: cobra.ArbitraryArgs` is the usual recipe.
4. **Pass-through env/cwd** — likely set `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`/cwd consistent with existing `external.Agent.run` (`external.go:438`) so `entire-pgr` sees the same context.
5. **Help/listing (optional)** — git scans `PATH` once for `git help -a`. You can skip this initially and add an eager scan later if `entire help` should list discovered plugins.

The main tradeoff is **lazy vs. eager discovery**. Lazy = zero startup cost, only resolves on use, but `entire help` won't list `pgr`. Eager = nicer help, costs a PATH scan on every invocation. Recommend starting lazy + adding a help integration later.

Here's how the three differ:

**git** — pure PATH-scan, lazy
- No registry, no manifest. When you type `git foo` and `foo` isn't built-in, git execvp's `git-foo` from PATH with the remaining args. That's it.
- `git help -a` does an on-demand PATH walk to list `git-*` binaries, but normal invocation doesn't.
- Process replacement via `execvp`, so signals/TTY just work.

**kubectl** — PATH-scan, lazy with explicit listing
- Same model as git: `kubectl foo` → `kubectl-foo` on PATH, exec'd with remaining args. Hyphens in the plugin name map to underscores in the binary (`kubectl foo-bar` → `kubectl-foo_bar`).
- Adds `kubectl plugin list` that walks PATH and reports conflicts/shadowing (built-ins always win, with a warning).
- Uses `os/exec`, not exec replacement.

**gh** — managed install dir, eager Cobra registration (`pkg/cmd/extension/`, `pkg/cmd/root/extension.go`, `pkg/cmd/root/root.go:191-203`)
- **Doesn't scan PATH at all.** Extensions live in `~/.local/share/gh/extensions/<gh-name>/` — a directory gh manages itself via `gh extension install/list/upgrade/remove`.
- At root build time, `em.List()` enumerates that dir; for each extension it builds a Cobra subcommand with `DisableFlagParsing: true` and `RunE` calling `em.Dispatch(args, stdin, stdout, stderr)`. The `Dispatch` does the actual `exec.Cmd` with piped I/O (`manager.go:91`).
- Conflict resolution is explicit: `cmd.Find([]string{name})` — if a built-in claims that verb, the extension is skipped (`root.go:197`).
- Extensions go into `GroupID: "extension"` so they get their own section in help.
- Disables auth check and telemetry per-extension (privacy: extension names may be sensitive). Also checks for extension updates async in PreRun/PostRun.
- Shell scripts are supported on Windows via `sh -c` shim (`manager.go:117`).

**Recommendation for `entire pgr`**

Given your existing `entire-agent-*` PATH scan is the established convention, the **kubectl model** is closest:
- Lazy `entire-<name>` PATH lookup, exec'd with the remaining args
- Skip if name collides with a built-in or with a registered agent
- Skip if it matches the `entire-agent-` prefix (reserved for the protocol)
- Add `entire plugin list` later if you want gh-style discoverability

Going gh-style (managed install dir + `entire extension install`) is heavier — you'd own download, version pinning, update notifications, an install registry. Probably overkill for now.

The git-style `execvp` is cleanest for signal/TTY handling but doesn't work on Windows; `os/exec` with stdin/stdout/stderr passthrough (what gh and kubectl do) is the safer cross-platform choice.

Yes, easily. The migration path is clean because the two approaches share the same execution shape — both end in `exec.Cmd` with stdin/stdout/stderr piped through.

What stays the same:
- `entire-pgr` binary contract (no protocol, just argv + I/O passthrough)
- Conflict rule (built-ins/agents win)
- `DisableFlagParsing: true` on the dispatch path
- `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT` / cwd plumbing

What changes when you go gh-style later:
- **Source of truth** flips from PATH to a managed dir (e.g. `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/`). The `LookPath`/scan call gets replaced with a `manager.List()` over that dir.
- **Registration** flips from lazy (resolve-on-unknown-arg) to eager (Cobra subcommands built at root construction). You add `cmd.AddCommand(...)` per plugin in a loop, mirroring `root.go:191-203`.
- **New surface area**: `entire plugin install/list/upgrade/remove` commands. This is the bulk of the work — not the dispatch itself.

Two things worth getting right *now* so the later switch is trivial:

1. **Put dispatch behind an interface.** Even if today's only impl is "look up `entire-<name>` on PATH", define something like `PluginResolver.Resolve(name) (path string, ok bool)` and `PluginRunner.Run(path, args, io)`. Later, `ManagedDirResolver` slots in alongside (or replaces) `PathResolver` without touching the Cobra wiring.
2. **Don't leak "PATH" into user-visible naming.** Call them "plugins" or "extensions" in help/errors, not "PATH plugins". That way the docs don't need rewriting when the storage location changes.

The risk if you skip the abstraction: it's small. Even without it, the dispatch site is ~30 lines and easy to refactor. So don't over-engineer — a single `dispatchPlugin(name, args)` function is fine, and you can extract an interface when the second implementation arrives.

One thing that *would* be a breaking change for users: if today `entire pgr` resolves `entire-pgr` from PATH, and tomorrow it only resolves from `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/`, users who installed via Homebrew/apt will be surprised. gh sidesteps this by never having had PATH discovery. If you want both to coexist long-term, the resolver chain (managed dir → PATH fallback) handles it, but you'd want to decide that policy before users build muscle memory.

Summary of what was added:
- **`cmd/entire/cli/plugin.go`** — kubectl-style dispatcher. Looks up `entire-<name>` on PATH when `<name>` isn't a built-in. Exit code propagates. Sets `ENTIRE_CLI_VERSION` and `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`. Skips `entire-agent-*` (reserved for the protocol).

Worth deciding before you ship:
- **Discovery for help.** `entire help` and `entire --help` won't list `entire-pgr`. kubectl adds `kubectl plugin list` for this — easy to add later if you want it.
- **Hyphen handling.** `entire foo-bar` resolves to `entire-foo-bar` literally (git-style). kubectl translates hyphens to underscores in the binary half. I went git-simple.
- **Telemetry.** Plugin invocations currently aren't tracked since the dispatcher exits before Cobra's `PersistentPostRun`. If you want plugin usage in telemetry (with care around privacy — gh disables telemetry for non-official extensions), that needs explicit wiring.
does gh disables the telemetry fully or at least track which plugins are used?

**Fully disabled.** No event at all — not even an anonymized "an extension was used" signal.

The implementation is annotation-based (`pkg/cmdutil/telemetry.go:50`):

```go
func DisableTelemetry(cmd *cobra.Command) {
    cmd.Annotations["telemetry"] = "disabled"
}
```

`RecordTelemetry` checks that annotation first and returns early, so no `command_invocation` event is recorded. The wiring in `pkg/cmd/root/extension.go:87`:

```go
if !extensions.IsOfficial(ext.Name(), ext.Owner()) {
    cmdutil.DisableTelemetry(cmd)
}
```

Their stated reasoning (comment in `extension.go:82-86`): extension names "can be arbitrary (potentially including sensitive identifiers such as project or organization names)" — so they don't even want the dimension carrying it.

**The "official" allowlist is tiny and hardcoded** (`pkg/extensions/official.go:25`):

```go
var OfficialExtensions = []OfficialExtension{
    {Name: "aw", Owner: "github", Repo: "gh-aw"},
    {Name: "stack", Owner: "github", Repo: "gh-stack"},
}
```

Two extensions, both owned by the `github` org, both checked owner-and-name (case-sensitive on name, case-insensitive on owner) — so a third-party `someuser/gh-stack` does *not* qualify even though the name matches. Only those two contribute their command path to telemetry.

**For your case, three options:**

1. **Match gh exactly** — fully disable telemetry for plugins. Simplest, most private. You lose visibility into plugin adoption.
2. **Track presence only** — record a `plugin_invocation` event with no name/args, just the fact that *a* plugin ran. Tells you "X% of users use plugins" without leaking which one. Mid-privacy.
3. **Allowlist** — like gh, hardcode a small set of known-safe plugin names (e.g. ones you ship yourself) that contribute their name to telemetry; everything else is silent.

Which one matches your appetite? Given you're following kubectl's structural model and gh's privacy posture is the strictest of the three, option 1 is the lowest-friction default. Option 3 makes sense if you plan to ship official Entire plugins yourself and want adoption metrics on them specifically.

Three commits, reviewer's gap closed. The new integration tests:

| Test | What it asserts about main.go's early dispatch |
|---|---|
| `HappyPath` | argv reaches plugin; stdout/stderr passthrough |
| `ExitCodePropagation` | child's non-zero exit reaches parent's `os.Exit` |
| `BuiltinWins` | dispatcher must defer to Cobra when name is built-in |
| `PluginNotFound` | dispatcher falls through cleanly to Cobra's unknown-command error |
| `FlagAfterPluginNameNotEatenByCobra` | confirms the dispatch happens *before* Cobra's flag parser sees `--help`/`--version` |
| `StdinPassthrough` | parent stdin reaches child plugin |
| `EnvVarsForwarded` | `ENTIRE_CLI_VERSION` is set in plugin env |
| `AgentProtocolBinarySkipped` | `entire-agent-*` binaries are reserved (defense in depth at the binary level) |
| `SigintReachesPlugin` *(Unix-only)* | parent's SIGINT handler → ctx cancel → `cmd.Cancel` → plugin trap fires; child cleans up rather than getting SIGKILL'd |

The signal test uses a readiness file (plugin writes `ready` after installing its trap, test waits for it before signalling) so the trap-install race is eliminated. Windows is left out of the signal coverage since the dispatcher's `cmd.Cancel = SIGINT` branch is Unix-only — on Windows the runtime falls back to `Process.Kill`, which is what gh, kubectl and the existing `external.Agent.run` also do.
